putnam-2005-a1.title: Strong induction
putnam-2005-a1.body:
We use strong induction on $n$; $n = 1 = 2^03^0$ is a representation. Let $n\ge2$ and assume every positive integer below $n$ has a representation (a sum of numbers $2^r3^s$, none dividing another — in particular all distinct).

**$n$ even.** Take a representation $\frac n2 = s_1 + \cdots + s_k$ and double it: $n = 2s_1+\cdots+2s_k$. Each $2s_i$ has the form $2^r3^s$, and $2s_i\mid 2s_j \iff s_i\mid s_j$, so no summand divides another.

**$n$ odd.** Let $3^k$ be the largest power of $3$ with $3^k\le n$, so $3^k \le n < 3^{k+1}$. If $n = 3^k$ we are done. Otherwise $n - 3^k$ is even and positive, and $\frac{n-3^k}{2} < n$ has a representation $s_1+\cdots+s_j$. Then
$$n = 3^k + 2s_1 + \cdots + 2s_j .$$
Check the conditions:
- the $2s_i$ do not divide each other (as above);
- $2s_i \nmid 3^k$, since $2s_i$ is even and $3^k$ is odd;
- $3^k\nmid 2s_i$: we have $2s_i \le n - 3^k < 3^{k+1} - 3^k = 2\cdot3^k$, so $0 < s_i < 3^k$; if $3^k\mid 2s_i$ then $3^k \mid s_i$ (as $\gcd(3^k,2)=1$), impossible.

This completes the induction. ∎ (E.g. $23 = 9 + 2\cdot7$ and $7 = 3 + 2\cdot 2$, $2 = 2\cdot1$, giving $23 = 9 + 2(3 + 4) = 9 + 6 + 8$.)

*Remark.* The representation need not be unique: $11 = 2 + 9 = 3 + 8$. The problem is due to Paul Erdős.

putnam-2005-a2.title: Recursion by removing the last column
putnam-2005-a2.body:
For $n = 1$ there is no such tour (it would have to start and end at the same point), so assume $n\ge2$. A rook tour is a path through all $3n$ points of the $n\times3$ grid using unit steps. Let $A_n$ be the set of tours from $(1,1)$ to $(n,1)$ and $B_n$ the set of tours from $(1,1)$ to $(n,3)$. We show $|A_n| = |B_n| = |A_{n-1}| + |B_{n-1}|$ for $n\ge2$.

**Tours in $A_n$.** The point $(n,3)$ is not an endpoint and has only the neighbours $(n-1,3)$ and $(n,2)$, so the tour uses both segments $(n-1,3)$–$(n,3)$–$(n,2)$. The point $(n,2)$ uses exactly one more segment, to $(n,1)$ or to $(n-1,2)$.
- If it goes to $(n,1)$, the tour ends with $(n-1,3),(n,3),(n,2),(n,1)$. Deleting the last three points gives a tour in $B_{n-1}$; conversely every tour in $B_{n-1}$ extends this way.
- If it goes to $(n-1,2)$, the tour contains the consecutive stretch $(n-1,2),(n,2),(n,3),(n-1,3)$, and the endpoint $(n,1)$ is reached from $(n-1,1)$. Replace the stretch by the single segment $(n-1,2)$–$(n-1,3)$ and delete the final point $(n,1)$: this gives a tour in $A_{n-1}$. Conversely, in a tour of $A_{n-1}$ the point $(n-1,3)$ is not an endpoint and has only the neighbours $(n-2,3)$, $(n-1,2)$, so the segment $(n-1,2)$–$(n-1,3)$ is used and the construction can be reversed. (For $n = 2$ this case does not occur, matching $A_1 = \emptyset$.)

So $|A_n| = |A_{n-1}| + |B_{n-1}|$.

**Tours in $B_n$.** Symmetrically, $(n,1)$ is not an endpoint, so the tour uses $(n-1,1)$–$(n,1)$–$(n,2)$, and $(n,2)$ continues either to $(n,3)$ (the tour ends $(n-1,1),(n,1),(n,2),(n,3)$; delete three points to get a tour in $A_{n-1}$) or to $(n-1,2)$ (replace the stretch $(n-1,1),(n,1),(n,2),(n-1,2)$ by the segment $(n-1,1)$–$(n-1,2)$ and delete the final $(n,3)$, which was reached from $(n-1,3)$, to get a tour in $B_{n-1}$). The reverse step needs the segment $(n-1,1)$–$(n-1,2)$ in every tour of $B_{n-1}$: for $n-1\ge2$ the point $(n-1,1)$ is not an endpoint and has only the neighbours $(n-2,1)$, $(n-1,2)$; for $n-1 = 1$ the only tour $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3)$ uses it. So $|B_n| = |A_{n-1}| + |B_{n-1}|$.

**Conclusion.** $|A_1| = 0$, $|B_1| = 1$, hence $|A_2| = |B_2| = 1$, and then $|A_n| = |B_n| = 2|A_{n-1}|$ for $n \ge 3$. Therefore $|A_n| = 2^{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$.

For example, for $n=3$ the two tours are $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3),(3,3),(3,2),(2,2),(2,1),(3,1)$ and $(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3),(3,3),(3,2),(3,1)$.

**Answer:** $2^{n-2}$ (for $n\ge2$; there are none for $n=1$).

putnam-2005-a3.title: Real part of the logarithmic derivative
putnam-2005-a3.body:
(Implicitly $n\ge1$, $z\ne0$, and any branch of $z^{n/2}$ may be used on a region avoiding $0$.) Since $\frac{d}{dz}z^{-n/2} = -\frac n2 z^{-n/2-1}$ for any branch,
$$g'(z) = z^{-n/2}\left(p'(z) - \frac{n}{2z}p(z)\right) = \frac{z^{-n/2}}{2z}\Big(2zp'(z) - np(z)\Big).$$
So the zeros of $g'$ are the nonzero zeros of $h(z) = 2zp'(z) - np(z)$, independent of the branch.

Write $p(z) = c\prod_{j=1}^n(z - r_j)$ with $|r_j| = 1$. Let $h(z) = 0$, $z\ne0$. If $p(z) = 0$, then $z$ is some $r_j$ and $|z| = 1$. Otherwise divide by $p(z)$: $\frac{zp'(z)}{p(z)} = \sum_j\frac{z}{z-r_j}$, so
$$0 = \frac{h(z)}{p(z)} = \sum_{j=1}^n\left(\frac{2z}{z-r_j} - 1\right) = \sum_{j=1}^n\frac{z+r_j}{z-r_j}.$$
For each $j$,
$$\frac{z+r_j}{z-r_j} = \frac{(z+r_j)(\bar z - \bar r_j)}{|z-r_j|^2} = \frac{|z|^2 - |r_j|^2 + (r_j\bar z - z\bar r_j)}{|z-r_j|^2},$$
and $r_j\bar z - z\bar r_j = w - \bar w$ (with $w = r_j\bar z$) is purely imaginary. Since $|r_j| = 1$,
$$0 = \operatorname{Re}\sum_j\frac{z+r_j}{z-r_j} = \left(|z|^2 - 1\right)\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{1}{|z-r_j|^2}.$$
The sum is positive, so $|z| = 1$. ∎

putnam-2005-a3.title: Rolle's theorem on the circle
putnam-2005-a3.body:
As in the first solution, it suffices to show that all roots of the degree-$n$ polynomial $h(z) = 2zp'(z) - np(z)$ lie on the unit circle (its leading coefficient is $(2n - n)c = nc \ne 0$, so it has exactly $n$ roots with multiplicity).

Write $r_j = e^{2i\theta_j}$. For $z = e^{2i\theta}$,
$$z - r_j = e^{i(\theta+\theta_j)}\left(e^{i(\theta-\theta_j)} - e^{-i(\theta-\theta_j)}\right) = 2i\,e^{i(\theta+\theta_j)}\sin(\theta-\theta_j),$$
so $g(e^{2i\theta}) = p(e^{2i\theta})e^{-in\theta} = K\,\varphi(\theta)$, with a nonzero constant $K$ (using the branch $z^{n/2} = e^{in\theta}$) and the real function $\varphi(\theta) = \prod_j\sin(\theta - \theta_j)$. Differentiating, $2ie^{2i\theta}g'(e^{2i\theta}) = K\varphi'(\theta)$.

On $[0,\pi)$, $\varphi$ has zeros exactly at the points $\theta_j \bmod \pi$, with total multiplicity $n$, and it is $\pi$-periodic up to sign. By Rolle's theorem (applied between consecutive distinct zeros, cyclically on a circle of length $\pi$, and counting a zero of multiplicity $k$ of $\varphi$ as a zero of multiplicity $k-1$ of $\varphi'$), $\varphi'$ has at least $n$ zeros (with multiplicity) per period of length $\pi$. These give at least $n$ zeros of $g'$, hence of $h$, on the unit circle, with multiplicity (distinct $\theta\in[0,\pi)$ give distinct $z = e^{2i\theta}$). Since $h$ has exactly $n$ roots, all of them lie on the unit circle. ∎

putnam-2005-a4.title: Length of a sum of rows
putnam-2005-a4.body:
Let $r_1,\dots,r_a$ be the rows of $H$ containing the all-ones $a\times b$ submatrix. Each row has squared length $r_i\cdot r_i = n$ (entries $\pm1$), and distinct rows are orthogonal. So for $v = r_1 + \cdots + r_a$,
$$|v|^2 = \sum_{i,j=1}^a r_i\cdot r_j = an .$$
In each of the $b$ columns of the submatrix, all $a$ rows have entry $1$, so $v$ has $b$ coordinates equal to $a$. Hence $|v|^2 \ge a^2b$. Therefore $an \ge a^2b$, i.e. $ab\le n$. ∎

putnam-2005-a4.title: A positive semidefinite matrix
putnam-2005-a4.body:
Permute rows and columns (this preserves orthogonality of rows) so that the all-ones block occupies the first $a$ rows and first $b$ columns. Let $M$ be the $a\times(n-b)$ matrix formed by the first $a$ rows and the last $n-b$ columns. For $i,j\le a$, the rows of $H$ are $(1,\dots,1,m_i)$, so
$$n\,\delta_{ij} = b + m_i\cdot m_j,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad MM^T = nI - bJ,$$
with $J$ the $a\times a$ all-ones matrix. For the all-ones vector $\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^a$, $J\mathbf 1 = a\mathbf 1$, so
$$0 \le |M^T\mathbf 1|^2 = \mathbf 1^TMM^T\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1^T(n - ab)\mathbf 1 = a(n-ab).$$
Hence $ab\le n$. ∎

*Remark.* Such $H$ is a Hadamard matrix; more generally (Lindsey's lemma) the entries of any $a\times b$ submatrix sum to at most $\sqrt{abn}$.

putnam-2005-a5.title: Substitute x = tan θ and use symmetry
putnam-2005-a5.body:
With $x = \tan\theta$, $dx = \sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $1 + x^2 = \sec^2\theta$:
$$I = \int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta .$$
Substitute $\theta\mapsto\frac\pi4 - \theta$ (which maps $[0,\frac\pi4]$ onto itself). Since
$$1 + \tan\left(\tfrac\pi4 - \theta\right) = 1 + \frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta} = \frac{2}{1+\tan\theta},$$
we get
$$I = \int_0^{\pi/4}\left[\ln2 - \ln(1+\tan\theta)\right]d\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\ln2 - I .$$
Hence $I = \dfrac{\pi\ln2}{8}$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac{\pi\ln 2}{8}\approx 0.2722$.

putnam-2005-a5.title: Double integral and symmetry
putnam-2005-a5.body:
For $x\in[0,1]$, $\ln(1+x) = \int_0^1\frac{x}{1+xy}\,dy$. So
$$I = \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{x}{(1+xy)(1+x^2)}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{y}{(1+xy)(1+y^2)}\,dy\,dx,$$
the second form by renaming $x\leftrightarrow y$ (the integrand is continuous, so Fubini applies). Adding the two forms and using $x(1+y^2) + y(1+x^2) = (x+y)(1+xy)$:
$$2I = \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{x+y}{(1+x^2)(1+y^2)}\,dy\,dx = 2\int_0^1\frac{x\,dx}{1+x^2}\int_0^1\frac{dy}{1+y^2} = 2\cdot\frac{\ln2}{2}\cdot\frac\pi4 .$$
So $I = \dfrac{\pi\ln2}{8}$.

putnam-2005-a6.title: Locate the first acute vertex
putnam-2005-a6.body:
Measure arcs as fractions of the circumference. With probability $1$ the points are distinct and no two are antipodal, so we ignore those cases. Label the vertices $Q_1,\dots,Q_n$ in counterclockwise order and let $g_i$ be the arc from $Q_i$ to $Q_{i+1}$ (indices mod $n$), so $\sum g_i = 1$.

**When is an angle acute?** The angle at $Q_i$ is an inscribed angle subtending the arc from $Q_{i+1}$ to $Q_{i-1}$ not containing $Q_i$, of length $1 - g_{i-1} - g_i$. So it equals $\pi(1-g_{i-1}-g_i)$, and it is acute iff $g_{i-1} + g_i > \frac12$.

**Structure.** If the angles at $Q_i$ and $Q_j$ are acute and $Q_i,Q_j$ are not adjacent, the pairs $\{g_{i-1},g_i\}$ and $\{g_{j-1},g_j\}$ are disjoint (here $n\ge4$ is used), so their total would exceed $1$: impossible. Hence the acute vertices are either none, one vertex, or two adjacent vertices (three would contain a non-adjacent pair). In particular, if some angle is acute, there is exactly one ordered pair of consecutive vertices $(Q, Q')$, $Q'$ following $Q$ counterclockwise, such that the angle at $Q'$ is acute and the angle at $Q$ is not.

**Computation.** So $\Pr(\text{some acute angle}) = \sum\Pr(E_{s,t})$ over ordered pairs $s\ne t$, where $E_{s,t}$ is the event "$P_t$ immediately follows $P_s$ counterclockwise, the angle at $P_t$ is acute and the angle at $P_s$ is not". By symmetry all $n(n-1)$ terms are equal to $\Pr(E_{1,2})$.

By rotation invariance put $P_1$ at position $0$; let $P_2$ be at position $x\in(0,1)$ (measured counterclockwise) and let the other $n-2$ points have smallest position $y_{\min}$ and largest position $y_{\max}$. Then $E_{1,2}$ says:
- $P_2$ follows $P_1$: all other points lie in $(x,1)$;
- angle at $P_2$ acute: $g(P_1\to P_2) + g(P_2\to\text{next}) = x + (y_{\min}-x) = y_{\min} > \frac12$;
- angle at $P_1$ not acute: $g(\text{previous}\to P_1) + g(P_1\to P_2) = (1 - y_{\max}) + x \le \frac12$, i.e. $y_{\max}\ge x + \frac12$.

If $x>\frac12$ the last condition is impossible. If $x\le\frac12$, the conditions say: all $n-2$ other points lie in $(\frac12,1)$, but not all in $(\frac12, x+\frac12)$. This has probability $2^{-(n-2)} - x^{n-2}$. Therefore
$$\Pr(E_{1,2}) = \int_0^{1/2}\left(2^{-(n-2)} - x^{n-2}\right)dx = \frac{1}{2^{n-1}} - \frac{1}{(n-1)2^{n-1}} = \frac{n-2}{(n-1)\,2^{n-1}},$$
and the answer is $n(n-1)\cdot\dfrac{n-2}{(n-1)2^{n-1}} = \dfrac{n(n-2)}{2^{n-1}}$.

*Check:* for $n=4$ this gives $1$; indeed opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $\pi$, so (unless both are right, probability $0$) one of them is acute.

**Answer:** $\dfrac{n(n-2)}{2^{n-1}}$.

putnam-2005-b1.title: floor(2a) is 2m or 2m+1
putnam-2005-b1.body:
Take
$$P(x,y) = (y - 2x)(y - 2x - 1),$$
which is a nonzero polynomial. Let $m = \lfloor a\rfloor$, so $m\le a < m+1$ and $2m\le 2a < 2m+2$.
- $2m$ is an integer $\le 2a$, so $2m\le\lfloor2a\rfloor$;
- $2m+2$ is an integer $>2a$, so $\lfloor 2a\rfloor \le 2m+1$.

Hence $\lfloor 2a\rfloor \in\{2m, 2m+1\}$, so one of the factors $y - 2x$, $y-2x-1$ vanishes at $(x,y) = (\lfloor a\rfloor,\lfloor2a\rfloor)$, and $P(\lfloor a\rfloor,\lfloor 2a\rfloor) = 0$ for every real $a$. ∎

(More precisely, $\lfloor 2a\rfloor = 2m$ if $a - m < \frac12$ and $2m+1$ otherwise. Any nonzero multiple of this $P$ also works.)

putnam-2005-b2.title: Cauchy–Schwarz bound, then cases
putnam-2005-b2.body:
By the Cauchy–Schwarz (or AM-HM) inequality,
$$(k_1+\cdots+k_n)\left(\frac1{k_1}+\cdots+\frac1{k_n}\right) \ge n^2,$$
so $5n - 4\ge n^2$, i.e. $(n-1)(n-4)\le0$, so $1\le n\le 4$. Order $k_1\le\cdots\le k_n$. For $n\ge2$ no $k_i$ equals $1$ (otherwise the reciprocals sum to more than $1$).
- **$n=1$:** $k_1 = 1$, which works ($1 = 5-4$).
- **$n=2$:** $k_1 + k_2 = 6$ with $2\le k_1\le k_2$: $(2,4)$ gives $\frac34$, $(3,3)$ gives $\frac23$. No solutions.
- **$n=3$:** $k_1+k_2+k_3 = 11$, so $2\le k_1\le 3$. The candidates are $(2,2,7)$, $(2,3,6)$, $(2,4,5)$, $(3,3,5)$, $(3,4,4)$, with reciprocal sums $\frac87$, $1$, $\frac{19}{20}$, $\frac{13}{15}$, $\frac56$. Only $(2,3,6)$ works.
- **$n=4$:** $5n-4 = 16 = n^2$, so equality holds in Cauchy–Schwarz, which forces $k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4$; then each is $4$, and indeed $4\cdot\frac14 = 1$.

**Answer:** $n=1,\ k_1 = 1$; $n = 3$ with $(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ any permutation of $(2,3,6)$; $n = 4$ with $k_1=k_2=k_3=k_4=4$.

putnam-2005-b2.title: Enumerate unit-fraction decompositions
putnam-2005-b2.body:
After obtaining $n\le4$ as in the first solution, list all solutions of $\frac1{k_1}+\cdots+\frac1{k_n} = 1$ with $k_1\le\cdots\le k_n$ and check the sum condition. For $n$ terms, $k_1\le n$ (the largest reciprocal is at least the average $\frac1n$).
- $n = 1$: $(1)$; sum $1 = 5\cdot1-4$. ✓
- $n = 2$: $k_1 = 2$ forces $k_2 = 2$: $(2,2)$, sum $4\ne6$.
- $n = 3$: $k_1\in\{2,3\}$. If $k_1 = 3$, then $(3,3,3)$. If $k_1 = 2$: $\frac1{k_2}+\frac1{k_3} = \frac12$ with $k_2\le 4$, $k_2 \ge 3$: $(2,3,6)$, $(2,4,4)$. Sums $9, 11, 10$; only $(2,3,6)$ has sum $11$. ✓
- $n = 4$: AM-HM equality forces $(4,4,4,4)$, sum $16$. ✓

Same answer as above.

putnam-2005-b3.title: Turn it into an ODE
putnam-2005-b3.body:
**Smoothness and sign.** Replacing $x$ by $a/x$, the condition reads
$$f'(x) = \frac{a}{x\,f(a/x)}\qquad(x>0). \tag{1}$$
The right side is differentiable (and positive), so $f'$ is differentiable and $f'>0$.

**Differentiate (1).** Since $\frac{d}{dx}\left[x f(a/x)\right] = f(a/x) - \frac ax f'(a/x)$,
$$f''(x) = -\frac{a\left[f(a/x) - \frac ax f'(a/x)\right]}{x^2f(a/x)^2}.$$
Eliminate the values at $a/x$ using (1), $f(a/x) = \frac{a}{xf'(x)}$, and the original equation, $\frac ax f'(a/x) = \frac{a}{f(x)}$:
$$f''(x) = -\frac{a\left[\frac{a}{xf'(x)} - \frac{a}{f(x)}\right]}{a^2/f'(x)^2} = -\frac{f'(x)}{x} + \frac{f'(x)^2}{f(x)} .$$
Multiply by $xf(x)$: $\;xf f'' + ff' - xf'^2 = 0$. Dividing by $f^2$,
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{xf'(x)}{f(x)}\right) = \frac{f'}{f} + \frac{xf''}{f} - \frac{xf'^2}{f^2} = 0 .$$
So $\frac{xf'(x)}{f(x)} = d$ is constant on the interval $(0,\infty)$, i.e. $(\ln f)' = \frac dx$, and $f(x) = cx^d$ with $c>0$. Since $f'>0$, $d>0$.

**Which of these work?** For $f = cx^d$: $f'(a/x) = cd\,a^{d-1}x^{1-d}$ and $\frac{x}{f(x)} = \frac{x^{1-d}}{c}$. So the equation holds for all $x$ iff
$$c^2d\,a^{d-1} = 1 .$$
If $d\ne1$, this is solved by $a = (c^2d)^{-1/(d-1)} > 0$, for every $c>0$. If $d = 1$ it says $c^2 = 1$, so $c = 1$ (and then any $a>0$ works).

**Answer:** all $f(x) = cx^d$ with $c>0$, $d>0$, except that $c$ must be $1$ when $d = 1$.

putnam-2005-b3.title: Logarithmic change of variables
putnam-2005-b3.body:
We know $f'>0$ from (1) of the first solution. Put $b = \ln a$, $x = e^{t}$ and $g(t) = \ln f(e^t)$, so $g'(t) = \frac{e^tf'(e^t)}{f(e^t)} > 0$, i.e. $f'(e^t) = e^{g(t) - t}g'(t)$. The equation $f'(a/x) = x/f(x)$ with $x = e^{b-s}$ (so $a/x = e^s$) becomes
$$e^{g(s)-s}g'(s) = e^{\,b - s - g(b-s)},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \ln g'(s) = b - g(s) - g(b-s).$$
The right side is unchanged under $s\mapsto b-s$, so $g'(s) = g'(b-s)$ for all $s$. Then $\frac{d}{ds}\left[g(s) + g(b-s)\right] = g'(s) - g'(b-s) = 0$, so $g(s)+g(b-s)$ is constant, hence $\ln g'(s)$ is constant: $g'(s) = d > 0$. So $g(t) = dt + \ln c$ and $f(x) = cx^d$. The verification step is as in the first solution. ∎

putnam-2005-b4.title: Count by the number of nonzero entries
putnam-2005-b4.body:
Let $f(m,n,k)$ be the number of tuples counted by $f(m,n)$ with exactly $k$ nonzero entries ($0\le k\le n$). To build one:
- choose the positions of the nonzero entries: $\binom nk$ ways;
- choose their signs: $2^k$ ways;
- choose their absolute values, an ordered $k$-tuple of positive integers $(y_1,\dots,y_k)$ with $y_1+\cdots+y_k\le m$. The partial sums $y_1 < y_1+y_2 < \cdots < y_1+\cdots+y_k$ form a $k$-element subset of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and every such subset arises from exactly one tuple; so there are $\binom mk$ ways.

Hence $f(m,n,k) = 2^k\binom nk\binom mk$ and
$$f(m,n) = \sum_{k\ge0}2^k\binom nk\binom mk,$$
which is symmetric in $m$ and $n$ (terms with $k>\min(m,n)$ vanish). So $f(m,n) = f(n,m)$. ∎

putnam-2005-b4.title: A symmetric recurrence

putnam-2005-b5.title: Peel off powers of x₁² + ⋯ + xₙ²
putnam-2005-b5.body:
Write $\Delta = \sum_i\partial^2/\partial x_i^2$ and $Q = x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2$.

**Reduction to homogeneous $P$.** $\Delta$ maps homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ to homogeneous polynomials of degree $d-2$, so $\Delta P = 0$ iff $\Delta P_d = 0$ for every homogeneous component $P_d$ of $P$. If $P = QS$, then $P_d = QS_{d-2}$ (compare components of degree $d$). So each $P_d$ satisfies both hypotheses, and it suffices to treat homogeneous $P$.

**Homogeneous case.** Suppose $P\ne0$ is homogeneous with $\Delta P = 0$ and $Q\mid P$. Write $P = Q^mR$ with $m\ge1$ as large as possible; then $R\ne0$ is homogeneous of some degree $e\ge0$ and $Q\nmid R$. We compute, using $\nabla Q = 2x$ and $x\cdot x = Q$:
$$\partial_i(Q^m) = 2mx_iQ^{m-1},\qquad \Delta(Q^m) = \sum_i\left(2mQ^{m-1} + 4m(m-1)x_i^2Q^{m-2}\right) = 2m(n + 2m - 2)\,Q^{m-1}.$$
By Euler's formula for the homogeneous $R$, $\sum_ix_i\,\partial_iR = eR$, so
$$\Delta(Q^mR) = \Delta(Q^m)R + 2\sum_i\partial_i(Q^m)\,\partial_iR + Q^m\Delta R = Q^{m-1}\Big[2m(n+2m-2)R + 4meR + Q\,\Delta R\Big].$$
Since $\Delta P = 0$ and the polynomial ring has no zero divisors,
$$2m(n + 2m - 2 + 2e)\,R = -Q\,\Delta R .$$
The constant $2m(n+2m-2+2e)$ is positive ($m\ge1$, $n\ge1$), so $Q$ divides $R$ — contradicting the maximality of $m$. Hence $P = 0$. ∎

putnam-2005-b5.title: Apply P to itself as a differential operator
putnam-2005-b5.body:
Write $P = \sum_\alpha c_\alpha x^\alpha$ (multi-indices $\alpha$, $x^\alpha = x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}$), and let $P(\partial) = \sum_\alpha c_\alpha\partial^\alpha$ be the differential operator obtained by substituting $\partial_i = \partial/\partial x_i$ for $x_i$. Constant-coefficient operators commute and multiply like polynomials, so if $P = Q\cdot S$ with $Q = \sum x_i^2$, then $P(\partial) = S(\partial)\,\Delta$ and
$$P(\partial)P = S(\partial)(\Delta P) = 0 .$$
Now evaluate $P(\partial)P$ at $x = 0$. For multi-indices $\beta,\alpha$, $\partial^\beta x^\alpha$ at $0$ equals $\alpha!$ if $\beta = \alpha$ and $0$ otherwise (if $\beta\ne\alpha$, either some $\beta_i>\alpha_i$ and the result is $0$, or the result is a nonconstant monomial). So
$$0 = \big(P(\partial)P\big)(0) = \sum_\alpha c_\alpha^2\,\alpha!,$$
and since the $c_\alpha$ are real, all $c_\alpha = 0$: $P = 0$. ∎

*Remark.* The result fails in characteristic $p$: $Q^p = \sum x_i^{2p}$ is harmonic there.

putnam-2005-b6.title: A determinant, integrated
putnam-2005-b6.body:
Let $J_x$ be the $n\times n$ matrix with $x$ on the diagonal and $1$ elsewhere. By the Leibniz formula,
$$\det J_x = \sum_{\pi\in S_n}\sigma(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^n(J_x)_{i,\pi(i)} = \sum_{\pi\in S_n}\sigma(\pi)\,x^{\nu(\pi)},$$
since the factor is $x$ exactly when $\pi(i) = i$.

On the other hand $J_x = (x-1)I + J$ with $J$ the all-ones matrix. $J$ has rank $1$ and trace $n$, so its eigenvalues are $n$ (once) and $0$ ($n-1$ times); hence $J_x$ has eigenvalues $x+n-1$ and $x-1$ ($n-1$ times), and
$$\det J_x = (x+n-1)(x-1)^{n-1}.$$
Integrate both expressions over $[0,1]$, using $\int_0^1x^\nu\,dx = \frac{1}{\nu+1}$, and substitute $y = 1-x$:
$$\sum_{\pi}\frac{\sigma(\pi)}{\nu(\pi)+1} = \int_0^1(x+n-1)(x-1)^{n-1}dx = (-1)^{n-1}\int_0^1(n-y)\,y^{n-1}dy = (-1)^{n-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n+1}\right) = (-1)^{n+1}\frac{n}{n+1}. \qquad ∎$$

putnam-2005-b6.title: Inclusion–exclusion on fixed-point sets
putnam-2005-b6.body:
For $U\subseteq[n] = \{1,\dots,n\}$ let $f(U)$ be the sum of $\sigma(\pi)$ over permutations whose set of fixed points is exactly $U$, and for $T\subseteq[n]$ let $g(T) = \sum_{U\supseteq T}f(U)$, the sum of $\sigma(\pi)$ over permutations fixing every point of $T$. Such permutations are the permutations of the remaining $n - |T|$ points, with the same sign; since a symmetric group on $\ge2$ symbols has equally many even and odd permutations,
$$g(T) = \begin{cases}1 & |T|\ge n-1,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
By Möbius inversion on subsets, $f(U) = \sum_{T\supseteq U}(-1)^{|T|-|U|}g(T)$. With $|U| = i$: the term $T = [n]$ contributes $(-1)^{n-i}$, and the $n-i$ sets $T\supseteq U$ of size $n-1$ contribute $(-1)^{n-1-i}$ each. So $f(U) = (-1)^{n-i}(1 - n + i)$.

Grouping permutations by their fixed-point set,
$$\sum_\pi\frac{\sigma(\pi)}{\nu(\pi)+1} = \sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni(-1)^{n-i}\frac{1-n+i}{i+1} = \sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni(-1)^{n-i} - \sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni(-1)^{n-i}\frac{n}{i+1}.$$
The first sum is $(1-1)^n = 0$. In the second, $\frac{1}{i+1}\binom ni = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{i+1}$, so it equals
$$\frac{n}{n+1}\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{j}(-1)^{n+1-j} = \frac{n}{n+1}\left[(1-1)^{n+1} - (-1)^{n+1}\right] = -(-1)^{n+1}\frac{n}{n+1}.$$
Hence the total is $(-1)^{n+1}\frac{n}{n+1}$. ∎
